case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the appropriate remedy for the unconstitutional non-uniformity of quarterly bankruptcy fees under 28 U.S.C. § 1930(a)(6), as recognized in Siegel v. Fitzgerald, requires the United States Trustee to refund excess fees paid by Chapter 11 debtors in districts outside North Carolina and Alabama.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 1930(a)(6) - the 2017 Amendment to the quarterly fee statute governing Chapter 11 bankruptcy cases, which was found unconstitutional in Siegel v. Fitzgerald for violating the Bankruptcy Clause's uniformity requirement, in conjunction with the Due Process Clause of the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The Office of the United States Trustee argues that refunding approximately $326 million in quarterly fees collected under the unconstitutional statute is not the appropriate remedy, contending that prospective relief is sufficient to cure the constitutional infirmity, that the financial burden on the federal government and taxpayers is prohibitively large, and that Congress's legislative intent to fund the bankruptcy system through user fees supports denying retrospective monetary relief to debtors who already paid the fees
case_analysis.respondent_position: John Q. Hammons and respondents argue that well-settled Supreme Court precedent, particularly McKesson Corp. v. Division of Alcoholic Beverages and Montana National Bank v. Yellowstone County, firmly establishes that the Due Process Clause mandates meaningful post-payment relief when fees or taxes are collected under an unconstitutional statute, that every circuit court to address this issue has rejected the government's arguments, that prospective-only relief fails to cure the constitutional harm already suffered, and that a refund of excess fees paid is the only legally sound remedy
key_precedents: Siegel v. Fitzgerald, 142 S. Ct. 1770 (2022) - Supreme Court case that unanimously held the 2017 quarterly fee amendment unconstitutional for lack of uniformity under the Bankruptcy Clause

McKesson Corp. v. Division of Alcoholic Beverages and Tobacco, 496 U.S. 18 (1990) - established that the Due Process Clause requires states to provide meaningful post-payment relief for taxes collected under an unconstitutional scheme

Montana National Bank v. Yellowstone County, 276 U.S. 499 (1928) - held that prospective invalidation alone does not cure the harm of unlawful tax collection and that refund of unlawfully exacted funds is required
Iowa-Des Moines National Bank v. Bennett, 284 U.S. 239 (1931) - reinforced the principle that national banks subjected to unconstitutional discriminatory tax rates are entitled to refunds

Landgraf v. USI Film Products, 511 U.S. 244 (1994) - established the framework for analyzing retroactivity of statutory amendments, distinguishing prospective fee increases from retroactive impositions
In re CF & I Fabricators of Utah, Inc., 150 F.3d 1233 (10th Cir. 1998) - prior Tenth Circuit ruling that quarterly fee amendments are prospective in nature
In re Buffets LLC, 979 F.3d 366 (5th Cir. 2020) - Fifth Circuit decision reasoning that quarterly fee increases are analogous to prospective property tax increases

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh's movement toward the Respondent position after engaging with Justice Gorsuch's point about McKesson explicitly rejecting the legislative-intent argument confirms that the strongest challenge to our position has been adequately answered by the existing precedential framework. Justice Alito's remaining concern about the Fourteenth versus Fifth Amendment structural distinction is the one point I take most seriously, but as Justice Barrett correctly observes, the underlying due process principle applies with equal logical force to federal actors, and the uniformity defect in the fee statute was not a close constitutional question once Siegel v. Fitzgerald was decided. I will write narrowly, emphasizing that this holding is limited to situations where Congress has collected fees under a statute subsequently found unconstitutional for non-uniformity, the excess amounts are quantifiable, and the injured parties are identifiable — preserving the 8-1 coalition while leaving broader questions for another day.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh's movement toward the Respondent position after engaging with the McKesson precedent reinforces my own analysis — his concession that McKesson explicitly rejected the legislative-intent argument, and that the constitutional injury was consummated at the moment of each unlawful exaction, tracks precisely the originalist reading I find most defensible. The Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause, as understood at the founding and through the Montana National Bank line of cases, requires that the government make whole those from whom it has extracted money without constitutional authority; there is no principled textual or historical basis for a federal carve-out simply because the fiscal consequences are large. Justice Alito's remaining argument — that the predeprivation access to courts available to sophisticated Chapter 11 debtors satisfies McKesson's footnote 21 — still fails under close scrutiny: a debtor who must choose between paying an unconstitutional fee or watching their reorganization proceeding collapse has not been afforded a meaningful predeprivation opportunity in any sense the Due Process Clause would recognize. The Constitution's commands do not bend to the Treasury's preferences, and I see no originalist basis for fashioning a prospective-only remedy that leaves the government holding $326 million it had no constitutional authority to collect.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas's originalist framing has moved me — he correctly identifies that I have no principled basis for creating a federal carve-out from McKesson simply because the fiscal consequences are substantial, and his point that the Constitution's commands do not yield to budgetary preferences is one I cannot easily dismiss from my own textualist methodology. Justice Gorsuch's observation that McKesson explicitly rejected the legislative-intent argument I was relying upon — that a legislature's preference for collecting higher fees cannot substitute for retrospective relief — directly forecloses my Morales-Santana analogy, since that case addressed prospective statutory reconstruction, not government retention of funds already collected under a void enactment. I remain genuinely troubled by the sovereign immunity and Fifth Amendment mapping questions that my colleagues have not fully resolved, and I believe the predeprivation opportunity argument retains some force that the majority underweights — sophisticated Chapter 11 debtors with counsel are not analogous to retail taxpayers facing a 'pay first, litigate later' scheme with no realistic alternative. However, I cannot in good conscience maintain that the government may retain $326 million extracted under a statute this Court unanimously struck down in Siegel when no structural impossibility prevents a straightforward refund remedy, and the weight of settled Due Process doctrine from Montana National Bank through McKesson ultimately compels me to join the Respondent position.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh's argument that McKesson's footnote 21 limits retrospective relief to situations where debtors lacked meaningful predeprivation opportunity deserves serious engagement, but I find it ultimately unpersuasive for two reasons: first, the practical ability to challenge fees in court before paying them does not constitute the kind of 'meaningful predeprivation process' McKesson contemplates when the constitutional defect is structural non-uniformity baked into the statute itself — no individual debtor's court challenge could have cured the Bankruptcy Clause violation; second, Justice Alito's invocation of Morales-Santana and legislative intent conflates the remedial question in citizenship cases, where leveling-up is structurally impossible, with a straightforward fee-refund context where the remedy is perfectly calibrated to the injury. The government's retention of $326 million extracted under a statute this Court unanimously struck down in Siegel would compound the constitutional injury and reward Congress for its own unconstitutional conduct — precisely what McKesson forbids. I am reinforced in this view by Justice Barrett's careful observation that the underlying due process principle applies with equal logical force to federal actors under the Fifth Amendment, and by the near-universal circuit consensus that prospective-only relief is constitutionally inadequate here.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh's movement toward the Respondent position after engaging with Justice Gorsuch's point about McKesson explicitly rejecting the legislative-intent argument confirms my view that the strongest challenge to our position has now been substantially answered within this conference. The predeprivation opportunity argument — which I acknowledged as the most serious challenge in round one — collapses under the weight of Justice Barrett's observation that the constitutional injury was fully consummated at the moment of each unlawful exaction, and Justice Jackson's point that the Bankruptcy Clause non-uniformity defect was not reasonably ascertainable to individual debtors at the time of payment. I write to emphasize that the Court's opinion should be written narrowly, as Chief Justice Roberts suggests, applying McKesson's settled principle to this specific fee-exaction context without broad pronouncements that could unsettle adjacent areas of federal fiscal law.

The separation-of-powers concern actually reinforces the Respondent's position: it is not the judiciary's role to relieve Congress of the fiscal consequences of its own unconstitutional legislation by fashioning a prospective-only remedy that leaves the constitutional injury unremedied.

Justice Roberts' minimalist framing — applying McKesson's settled Due Process principle narrowly to federal fee exactions under the Fifth Amendment without broad pronouncements — is the approach I find most institutionally sound, as it preserves the constitutional floor while limiting the holding's reach. The $326 million consequence remains troubling to me as a practical matter, but I cannot in good conscience hold that fiscal inconvenience overrides what McKesson establishes as a constitutional minimum.

Allowing the government to retain those unlawfully exacted funds would compound the constitutional injury and undermine the foundational principle that no one — including the federal government — may benefit from its own unconstitutional conduct at the expense of vulnerable debtors already navigating financial distress.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The constitutional violation here is clear after Siegel v. Fitzgerald, and the Due Process framework established in McKesson Corp. v. Division of Alcoholic Beverages & Tobacco creates a strong presumption favoring meaningful post-payment relief when fees were collected under an unconstitutional scheme without adequate predeprivation process. Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The text of the Due Process Clause and the Court's own precedents in McKesson Corp. and Montana National Bank establish a clear constitutional command: when the government collects fees or taxes under an unconstitutional scheme without providing a meaningful predeprivation hearing, it must afford meaningful post-payment relief. The Petitioner's legislative-intent argument fares no better — McKesson explicitly rejected the identical contention that a legislature's preference for collecting higher fees from everyone, rather than fewer parties, could substitute for constitutionally required retrospective relief. Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: While Siegel v. Fitzgerald correctly identified the constitutional uniformity violation, the appropriate remedy question is distinct and more nuanced.
